**Answer: 432**

**Setup.** Color the board like a checkerboard. Diagonal cells $(k,k)$ have $i+j$ even, so all eight share one color. Consecutive numbers alternate colors, so the diagonal numbers all have the same parity.

**Separation.** Removing the diagonal splits the off-diagonal cells into an upper and a lower triangle of 28 cells each. Any step from one triangle to the other must pass through a diagonal cell. So between two consecutive diagonal visits, the path stays in a single triangle.

**Color counts per triangle.** Each triangle has 16 cells with $i+j$ odd and 12 cells with $i+j$ even (off-diagonal).

**Case B: diagonal numbers are even.** Then odd numbers sit on the $i+j$ odd cells and even numbers on the $i+j$ even cells. Let $a_1$ be the smallest diagonal number. The numbers $1,\dots,a_1-1$ form one segment inside one triangle, and it contains $\lfloor (a_1-1)/2\rfloor$ even numbers. Each triangle has only 12 off-diagonal even-colored cells, so $\lfloor (a_1-1)/2\rfloor \le 12$, giving $a_1 \le 26$.

The diagonal sum is at most $a_1$ plus the seven largest remaining even numbers, which is at most
$$26 + (64+62+\cdots+52) = 26 + 406 = 432.$$

**Case A: diagonal numbers are odd.** The same argument applied to odd numbers gives $a_1 \le 25$. The sum is then at most $25 + (63+61+\cdots+51) = 25+399 = 424 < 432$.

**Achievability.** The bound 432 is attained by the diagonal set $\{26, 52, 54, \dots, 64\}$. Numbers $1$–$25$ fill one triangle, $27$–$51$ fill the other, and the odd numbers $53, 55, \dots, 63$ fill the remaining three cells of each triangle as single connectors between consecutive diagonal cells. The color counts match exactly in both triangles. I checked the counting constraints but did not construct an explicit board, so this final step rests on the known result for this problem rather than a verified example.

ANSWER: 432
